paragraphs.heading: What genetics studies
paragraphs.text: Genetics is the study of genes, of genetic variation and of heredity, the patterns by which traits are handed down from parents to offspring. It is an important part of biology because heredity is vital to how organisms evolve. Modern genetics also looks at how genes work and behave, studying them inside the cell, in whole organisms and across populations. It has many branches, among them molecular genetics, epigenetics, population genetics and paleogenetics.

paragraphs.heading: Genes and surroundings
paragraphs.text: Genes do not act alone: they work together with an organism's environment and experiences to shape how it develops and behaves, a pairing often called nature versus nurture. A classic example uses two genetically identical seeds of corn. One is planted where the climate is mild and one where it is dry. Their genes set the average height they could reach, but the plant in the dry place grows only half as tall, because it lacks water and nutrients.

paragraphs.heading: Mendel's peas
paragraphs.text: Gregor Mendel, a friar working in Brno in the 1800s, was the first to study genetics scientifically. Working with pea plants, he traced how certain traits were passed on and described the patterns with mathematics, presenting his paper in 1865. He saw that the plants inherited traits through separate units of inheritance, a term still used for what we call a gene. His work suggested that heredity comes in particles rather than being acquired, and that simple rules and ratios could explain how many traits are inherited.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas Mendel overturned
paragraphs.text: People made use of inheritance long before science explained it, breeding better crops and animals since prehistoric times. In the 1800s a popular idea was blending inheritance, in which offspring get a smooth mix of their parents' traits. Mendel found cases where traits plainly did not blend after crossing, which pointed to distinct genes instead. What looks like blending is now explained by several genes with quantitative effects. Another idea, often linked to Lamarck, held that children inherit traits their parents strengthened, and it is now known to be wrong.

paragraphs.heading: A forerunner
paragraphs.text: Before Mendel, the Hungarian noble Imre Festetics was the first to use the word genetic about heredity, and he is considered the first geneticist. In 1819 he described several rules of inheritance. He concluded from observation that organisms inherit their characteristics rather than acquire them. He also proposed that traits of past generations could reappear later.

paragraphs.heading: Finding genes on chromosomes
paragraphs.text: Mendel's importance was not widely grasped until 1900, by which time he had died; that year Hugo de Vries and other scientists rediscovered his research. William Bateson coined the word genetics in 1905. Scientists then hunted for the molecules in cells that carry inheritance. Nettie Stevens, studying mealworms, found that females had only the X chromosome while males had both X and Y, and concluded that sex depends on chromosomes and is set by the male. In 1911 Thomas Hunt Morgan argued that genes sit on chromosomes, based on a sex-linked white-eye mutation in fruit flies.
